key_points: GDPNow jumped to ~4.0% annualized for Q3, re-accelerating from 1.5%; private final demand firm, AI capex strong, consumer spending firming per FOMC minutes.

Michigan sentiment rebounded +5.7 to 55.2 (still low in level); initial claims at 206k signal no labor-driven slowdown in activity; easier bank lending standards for fourth straight quarter support credit-financed growth.
Strong growth backs the hike pricing for September and pushes both 2y and 10y yields higher; curve effect ambiguous (bear-flattening via Fed vs term premium), so near neutral on 2s10s.

Growth momentum is mildly positive for equities, oil demand, and the dollar via rate differentials, and mildly negative for gold, VIX, and HY spreads, though spreads and VIX are already near 1y lows, limiting the signal.
Risks to this view: staff saw growth risks skewed to the downside and minutes flag AI-repricing risk; payrolls were flat in July, so signals kept modest.
July CPI rose only ~0.08% m/m (index 332.57 to 332.81); y/y still ~3.3%, so momentum is soft while the level stays elevated.
June core PCE rose ~0.13% m/m (~1.6% annualized); y/y ~3.3%, consistent with the staff estimate and a gradual stepdown.
Market had priced a September hike and another by Q1; soft monthly prints raise the odds that hike pricing fades, a mild downside bias for 2y yields and the dollar, and a slight steepening bias.
The FOMC sees inflation risks skewed up (broad-based, AI demand, Middle East energy), with three hawkish dissents, which limits how far the disinflation signal can go.

Breakevens jumped 7bp in a week with oil's rebound, but long-run compensation is anchored and staff project H2 disinflation as gasoline falls, so breakevens are roughly neutral to slightly lower over 3m.
Softer inflation implies lower real yields, mildly supportive for equities and gold and mildly negative for VIX and HY spreads; the effect is small.
Labor signals are mixed but net firm. July payrolls were -23k, yet unemployment fell to 4.1% and claims are very low at 206k (224k a year ago).
The flat payroll print alongside a falling jobless rate points to slow labor-force growth rather than weak demand. The labor market looks balanced to tight, which is consistent with the minutes.

A firm labor market removes any labor-based argument for Fed easing and keeps the hawkish dissents (three votes for a hike) credible. That is a mild upward bias for front-end yields and modest bear flattening of 2s10s.
Wage growth of 3.5% y/y is moderate, so this is not a wage-price spiral signal. That limits the size of any tilt, and the effect on breakevens is minimal.
Stable employment supports earnings and credit: slightly tighter HY spreads and a marginally lower VIX. This is partly offset by hawkish-rate risk for equities.
The early-September jobs report ahead of the Sept 16 FOMC is the key labor catalyst. Another weak payroll headline is the main risk to this mildly hawkish read.
Fed funds at 3.50-3.75% (EFFR ~3.63%) while 2y is 4.24%: market prices roughly two 25bp hikes, with a September hike largely priced as of the July minutes.

FOMC majority (9-3) held in July; minutes say most supported holding and tightening 'likely necessary if inflation did not decline' - conditional, not a commitment. Desk survey median saw no change through 2027.

Incoming data lean against a September hike: July payrolls -23k, headline PCE estimated down to 3.7% and core to 3.3%, staff sees inflation declining in H2. Risk is that the Fed underdelivers versus pricing at the Sept 16 SEP.

Implication: front-end yields skew lower over 1m/3m, curve bull-steepens, dollar softens modestly, mild support for equities, gold and credit; breakevens slightly firmer if Fed seen tolerating inflation.
Hawkish tail remains (three hawkish dissents, 'will deliver price stability' language, GDPNow 4%), so tilts are kept moderate; 1w signal near neutral with no scheduled Fed event.

The 10y sits at a 1y high (99th percentile). Over the past month 2s10s steepened 13bp while the 2y fell. That pattern points to a rising term premium rather than policy expectations, consistent with heavy coupon supply and large deficits.

Coupon supply is dense: 2/5/7y auctions at end-August, 3/10/30y in September, and the November refunding (early Nov) within the 3m window. With no sign of cuts in coupon sizes, the supply pressure tilts mildly toward higher long yields and a steeper curve.
Fed reserve-management bill purchases absorb front-end supply and anchor the 2y. Supply effects on the 2y are therefore roughly neutral.

The FOMC balance-sheet task force is discussing the maturity composition of Fed Treasury holdings, under a chair who favors a smaller footprint. A shift toward bills would push more duration onto private hands, an upside risk to the term premium over 3m.

Mid-September tax receipts and fiscal-year-end TGA swings are a modest liquidity drag. The second-order effects of a higher term premium are slightly negative for equities and credit spreads and slightly positive for gold. The dollar gets a mild negative from fiscal-credibility concerns.

Speculative shorts in TY are extreme (3rd percentile), likely basis-trade related. Supply-driven upside in yields is therefore modest and could be offset by short-covering; signals are kept close to 0.50.

Financial conditions are very loose: NFCI -0.56, HY OAS 2.70% at the 9th percentile of its 1y range, SLOOS easing for a fourth straight quarter, and corporate bond and equity issuance strong. That supports risk assets in the near term.
With spreads this tight and VIX at the 11th percentile, the upside is asymmetric: spread widening and vol spikes are more likely than further compression over 1-3 months.
Funding markets are calm. Ample reserves, ongoing bill reserve-management purchases (WALCL up about $100bn y/y) and repo softness only briefly moving EFFR mean no funding-stress signal.

Vulnerabilities are building: hedge fund leverage near record highs, record repo and prime-brokerage borrowing, private credit redemptions rising, and leveraged AI capex financing. These are tail risks that add to the spread and VIX upside skew.

Fed participants said financial conditions may not be restrictive enough. That is a mild hawkish lean that could push yields up and tighten conditions, a small upward tilt for front-end and 10y yields.

The dollar is down 2.1% over the past month and sits at the 9th percentile of its 1y range. Loose global liquidity and the Fed balance sheet expansion lean slightly toward further dollar weakness and slight support for gold.
No meaningful liquidity signal for oil, breakevens or the 2s10s curve.

The 10-year T-note spec net short is about -947k contracts, at the 3rd percentile of the past year. With the 10y yield at the 99th percentile of its range, the trade is crowded, so short-covering risk tilts the odds toward lower 10y yields.
2-year shorts were covered heavily (+94k, 99th percentile, least short of the year), so there is little squeeze fuel left at the front end. A 10y-led squeeze would flatten 2s10s.
Dollar index specs are net long at the 95th percentile while the broad dollar sits at the 9th percentile of its range. Longs are offside and liquidation could extend dollar weakness.

Complacency signals: VIX at 15 (11th percentile), VIX futures net short near the 20th percentile, HY OAS at 2.70 (9th percentile). The minutes note hedge fund leverage near record highs. Mean reversion favours a higher VIX and wider spreads.
ES positioning is near flat and not crowded, so the equity signal is only mildly negative, via the vol and leverage vulnerability.
Gold longs are fairly crowded (74th percentile, 55% of open interest), a mild negative. Oil positioning (62nd percentile) and breakevens give essentially no signal.

Broad dollar fell 2.1% over the past month to the 9th percentile of its 1y range even as US yields rose, suggesting rest-of-world dynamics (foreign growth pickup, foreign yields rising in step) are outweighing the US rate-gap support.

Fed minutes: growth abroad picked up in Q2, foreign headline inflation above target from energy; foreign central banks holding but with upside inflation risk, so AFE yields tend to rise with US yields — global term premium pressure leans US 10y higher and the curve slightly steeper.
Speculative dollar longs at the 95th percentile leave the dollar vulnerable to further unwinding as the foreign growth story improves; mild bearish dollar tilt across horizons.
Weaker dollar is modestly supportive for gold, oil and US multinationals' earnings; continued foreign inflows into US equities mildly support SP500 and keep credit/vol calm.
Signals are modest; this factor alone does not justify large deviations from 0.50.
WTI at $87 sits well above its year-ago level (+35%) but 13% below its level three months ago and far off the $114 peak. That fits a Middle East risk premium that has partly bled out.
The +3.8% weekly bounce came alongside a +7bp rise in 10y breakevens. Near-term pass-through to breakevens and front-end hike pricing is mildly positive.

A conflict-driven curve is probably backwardated, and Fed staff expect lower retail gasoline in H2. Both imply a modest downward drift in spot oil at 1-3 months. The distribution stays right-skewed on escalation risk, so the tilt is small.
Speculative crude length is only mid-range (62nd percentile) after a +23k weekly add. Positioning is not extreme in either direction.
Effects on equities, the dollar (the US is a net energy exporter), HY spreads (energy issuers) and VIX from this factor alone are second-order, so those targets stay near 0.50.
Gold has rebounded 6.7% over the past month on geopolitical hedging, with spec length at the 74th percentile. This gives only a slight upward lean.

The Middle East conflict re-escalated, per the July minutes. WTI is up 3.8% on the week but 13% below three months ago, so a risk premium is rebuilding with upside skew. Two-way risk remains, since a de-escalation could knock oil back toward its range lows.

Risk pricing is complacent relative to geopolitical tail risk: the VIX is at the 11th percentile and HY spreads at the 9th. Shocks are asymmetric, which gives mild upside for the VIX, spreads and gold and mild downside for the S&P 500.
US midterm elections fall on 2026-11-03, inside the 3m window. Event and fiscal uncertainty typically lifts volatility into the vote and modestly favours term premium and curve steepening.

Rates get mixed signals from this factor. A flight to quality pulls yields down, but oil-driven inflation in a Fed with three hike dissents leans hawkish on the front end. Net is near neutral, with a slight lean to lower 10y yields on risk-off and slightly higher breakevens.
Newly announced tariffs are seen by participants as having modest inflation effects, a minor input. The dollar has only a small safe-haven bid against a weakening trend.

thesis: The 2y at 4.24% versus EFFR of about 3.63% prices roughly two hikes. Soft July CPI, a soft June core PCE print, flat payrolls and the desk survey median all argue the Fed under-delivers relative to that pricing at the Sept 16 SEP. That leans the 2y lower over 1-3m. The long end is held up by coupon supply, a global term premium, midterms and a possible balance-sheet maturity shift, and that is partly offset by extreme TY shorts. Net, the curve bias is to steepen, with only a mild upward tilt in 10y yields. The dollar is weak at the 9th percentile of its 1y range with crowded spec longs and narrowing rate expectations, so it tilts lower; I shrink the pooled signal toward 0.5. Equities are supported by 4% GDPNow, loose conditions and drift. The VIX at 15 and HY OAS at 2.70 are near 1y lows, with hedge-fund leverage and geopolitical tail risk, so mean reversion favors modestly higher vol and spreads. Gold gains from a softer dollar, a fading hike path and geopolitics. Oil is two-way: the risk premium is rebuilding, but backwardation and the staff's lower-gasoline call leave it near neutral at 3m. Breakevens are slightly firmer near term with oil.
